steps.title: Listen to three sentences from a food market.

items.text: We don't have any bread, but we have some rice.

steps.title: Look at the two groups of words.
steps.prompt: What is different about the second group?
steps.why: You cannot say two breads or three rices. These are uncountable.
steps.html:
You can count them: a lemon — two lemons · a mushroom — some mushrooms · an olive — six olives

You can't count them: bread · rice · yoghurt · honey · water

steps.title: Countable and uncountable
steps.html:
CountableUncountable
Exampleslemon, mushroom, olive, pearbread, rice, yoghurt, honey, beef
Singulara lemon—
Pluraltwo lemons— (no plural)
PositiveThere are some lemons.There's some rice.
NegativeThere aren't any lemons.There isn't any rice.
QuestionAre there any lemons?Is there any rice?

An uncountable noun always takes the singular verb: The rice is ready.

To count it, put a container in front: a bottle of water, a kilo of beef, a piece of cake.

Learners often write a bread or two rices. Use some bread and two bags of rice.

steps.title: some and any
steps.html:
UseExample
somepositive sentencesWe have some rice.
anynegatives and questionsWe don't have any bread. Is there any bread?
someoffers and requestsWould you like some water? Could I have some rice?

some and any work with both plural and uncountable nouns.

In an offer or a request, some is normal even in a question.
